description: A team of aspiring scientists trying to uncover the secrets of the arcane universe
summary:
Piercer is an interactive 3D documentary built on radar data from the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission. Clouds, smoke, and night hide the ground from ordinary satellite cameras exactly when it changes most; radar sees through all three. On a 3D globe, Piercer flies to three places that changed in 2026 at three speeds: an ice-and-rock collapse that sent a flood 59.5 km down Nepal's Bhote Koshi valley in minutes, a wildfire that burned 1,810 km² in Oregon over weeks, and the rainy season that turned the coastal plain of Jazan, Saudi Arabia, green.

Each place plays on a timeline that sets what NISAR recorded beside what photos could, or could not, show. Five days after the Nepal flood, radar showed 38% of the flood corridor had changed, five weeks before the first clear photo. In Oregon, photos look green again while the radar shrub signal is still at 51% of its pre-fire level. Every number is labelled measured, derived, reported or estimated, so anyone can check a finding against the data.
details:
GitHub

What it does

Piercer is an interactive 3D documentary about how radar sees change on Earth's surface when cameras cannot. A landing page explains how NISAR's radar works; then a 3D globe opens with three places that changed in 2026 at three speeds:

  • Minutes: Bhote Koshi, Nepal. An ice-and-rock collapse sent a flood surge 59.5 km down the valley on 26 August. Five days later, NISAR radar showed 38% (31–46%) of the flood corridor had changed against 7% of the slopes beside it, five weeks before the first clear photo. Photos later confirmed 11.7 km² of stripped ground.
  • Weeks: Big Grass Fire, Oregon–Idaho. Lightning on 23 July; 1,810 km² burned by late August. By October the photos look green again, but the radar shrub signal where it burned hottest is at 51% of its pre-fire level (81% outside).
  • A season: Jazan, Saudi Arabia. 169 mm of rain from June to November turned the coastal plain green, the coast last. 1,390 km² (a third of the plain) was newly green by 1 November, and ground the dawn radar kept flagging was 2.2–2.9 times as likely to turn green.

Each place has six chapters. The camera flies to a viewpoint chosen for the evidence, time plays where the story needs it (the surge minute by minute, the fire day by day, the season week by week), and you can take over at any moment: drag, zoom, scrub the timeline, switch layers (photo, false colour, radar change, wet ground) and the dusk or dawn radar pass. A finale puts all three on one timeline with every NISAR pass.

How it works

Our research pipeline (Python) turns NISAR L2 GUNW coherence and L2 GCOV backscatter into change maps. Every number has a stated rule, a control area to compare against, and a range from nudging the threshold. Photos (HLS), rainfall (GPM IMERG) and fire detections (VIIRS) explain what the radar saw. The web app reprojects these layers from UTM onto a three.js globe and drapes them on Copernicus DEM terrain. The on-screen text reads its numbers from the data files, and automated checks recompute them, so the words cannot drift from the evidence.

Benefits and intended impact

Disasters happen under cloud, smoke and darkness, exactly when optical satellites are blind. Piercer shows the public, students, responders and planners what radar can see in those moments, and teaches them to read radar evidence honestly: every statement is labelled measured, derived, reported, estimated or interpretation. It is built so a non-expert can follow the story and an expert can check every number.

Tools and languages

Python for the analysis; TypeScript, React 19, three.js and Vite for the app; zustand, proj4, geotiff.js and sharp for state, projections, GeoTIFFs and imagery. It runs in any modern browser, including phones.

What makes it creative

One season told at three speeds of change (minutes, weeks, a season), radar and photos side by side so the gap between them is the story, and an evidence label on every number so the documentary never overstates what the data shows.

What we considered

  • NISAR products are provisional (validated versions start 21 October 2026), so findings are given as ranges with controls.
  • There is no NISAR data from 27 July to 10 August 2026; the app shows the gap instead of hiding it.
  • Radar shows that the surface changed, not why; causes come from photos, rain, terrain and official reports.
  • Accessibility: full keyboard control, reduced-motion mode, and a phone layout.
